newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian parties back tough IMF reform programme.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian parties back tough IMF reform programme.

text.p: Leaders of Bulgaria's main political parties pledged their backing for an IMF reform programme on Tuesday, and President Petar Stoyanov appealed to Bulgarians to get to work to make it succeed.

"Today the main political forces of Bulgaria declared before me their support for the actions of the cabinet in concluding an agreement with the International Monetary Fund and their willingness once the new parliament is formed to pass all the laws needed for implementation of this agreement," Stoyanov said in a televised address.
"This is the event which will determine the course of Bulgaria's economic reform for years ahead.

"But the signature of the politicians means nothing without the efforts of all Bulgaria's citizens. To endure the crisis is not enough, to survive the poverty is not enough, not to hinder the future of Bulgaria is still not enough. You have to believe me -- we need a bit more effort to succeed."
The IMF and Bulgaria's interim cabinet announced on Monday an accord on financial reform and funding worth more than $650 million to stabilise the shattered economy over the next year.
The interim cabinet took office last month after 30 days of street protests fuelled by economic hardship toppled the former Socialist government of Zhan Videnov.

"We restored the national dignity of the country. Across the world people began to talk about Bulgaria with respect. We did this together. We managed to restore the chances which we lost during the last four years of political selfishness and shortsightedness," Stoyanov said.
The interim cabinet has the support of the Union of Democratic Forces, which is expected to form the next government after elections on April 19.
Socialist leader Georgi Parvanov, who replaced Videnov as party chief, told reporters his party leadership backed the IMF accord in principle.
Stoyanov said confidence in the new cabinet had halted the collapse of the lev currency, which recovered from February's historic lows of 3,000 to the dollar to trade around 1,600 now.
Monthly inflation soared to 242.7 percent in February but is forecast to fall below 50 percent in March, due partly to the lev recovery, but also consumers' shrinking buying power.
Unemployment is already 13.7 percent of the workforce, and the National Labour Exchange said on Tuesday the number of jobless could rise to 700,000 by June from February's 525,148.
Bulgaria's authorities have agreed to a tough programme of restructuring, privatisation and budget discipline, including implementation of a fixed exchange rate regime from June.
"I am appealing to all enterprising Bulgarians -- we have to get started," Stoyanov said.

"Bulgaria's dream factory is already closed, but it's time to open the real factories. It won't happen immediately but the desire for change is our greatest capital and this is why I believe we are going to make it. Today it's time to succeed."
